295.title: The Singh Sabha, 1873
295.hook: Sikhs found reform societies to teach Gurmukhi and renew Sikh practice
295.howItsDone: Many gurdwaras run Punjabi and Gurmukhi classes for children, a practice that grew from the Singh Sabha movement's schools; Khalsa College in Amritsar, founded in 1892, is one of its best-known legacies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, annexation: far from home. Today, how a community that had lost its kingdom found its feet again.

A grandparent's language, and grandchildren who don't speak it anymore. At first nobody notices. The kids answer in English, the recipes stop being written down, the old songs are hummed but not sung. Then one day somebody realizes: if we don't teach this now, it's gone. Many Sikhs had that feeling in the decades after 1849. The kingdom was gone. Schools, jobs and prestige ran in other languages. And a handful of people decided to do something. Today: the Singh Sabha.
screen: `A GRANDPARENT'S LANGUAGE.` → `IF WE DON'T TEACH IT NOW, IT'S GONE.` → `A FEW PEOPLE DECIDE TO ACT.`

segments.voice: Sabha means an assembly, a society; Singh is the name every Khalsa man carries. The first Singh Sabha was founded in Amritsar in 1873. It's often said to have been sparked when four Sikh students at a mission school in Amritsar announced they would become Christians. Many Sikhs felt they were losing touch with their own tradition, and asked why. Their answer was mostly not protest. It was school. The Singh Sabhas, soon dozens of them across Punjab and beyond, set out to teach Sikhs their own faith. They taught Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib, so people could read the Gurus' words for themselves. They printed books, tracts and newspapers in Punjabi, opened schools, and in 1892 helped found Khalsa College in Amritsar. Their scholars wrote histories, dictionaries and commentaries. One of them, Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, spent years helping Max Arthur Macauliffe, an Irish-born official who had left the colonial service, translate the Sikh scriptures into English. His six-volume work came out in 1909; it's old enough now that anyone may quote it freely, which is why this path names it as its English source. Not everyone in the movement agreed. Different Singh Sabhas argued, sometimes fiercely, about what Sikh practice should be, and historians still discuss how the movement reshaped Sikh identity. But its central idea was simple, and it lasted: a community renews itself by teaching its children to read its own words. Many weekend Punjabi classes at gurdwaras around the world today stand in that line.

The Gurmukhi alphabet is sometimes called the painti, the thirty-five, for its thirty-five letters, and its first letter is ura: say it once, OO-raa; it carries vowel sounds, like the oo in Guru. If the screen shows it, look at its shape for a few breaths and trace it in the air with a finger, and you'll know the first letter of the script the Guru Granth Sahib is written in.

296.title: Saragarhi, 1897
296.hook: twenty-one Sikh soldiers hold a signal post against thousands on the frontier
296.howItsDone: Sikhs and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army mark Saragarhi Day each year on 12 September; memorial gurdwaras for the twenty-one stand in Amritsar and Ferozepur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Singh Sabha: renewal begins at school. Today, twenty-one men at a lonely hilltop post.

Some jobs look small until the moment they aren't. The lifeguard watching an empty pool all summer. The night nurse checking the same monitors. The person keeping a signal lamp lit on a hill so two forts can talk to each other. Nobody writes songs about the quiet days. But on a September morning in 1897, on a ridge on the northwest frontier, the quiet job became the whole world for twenty-one men.
screen: `JOBS THAT LOOK SMALL.` → `A SIGNAL POST BETWEEN TWO FORTS.` → `SEPTEMBER, 1897.`

segments.voice: Garhi means a small fort. Saragarhi was a little stone post on the Samana ridge, in the mountains of what is now northwest Pakistan. Its job: pass signals by heliograph, flashes of sunlight from a mirror, between two larger British forts that couldn't see each other. Twenty-one soldiers of the 36th Sikhs, a Sikh regiment of the British Indian Army, held it under Havildar Ishar Singh. The region was in revolt; local Pashtun tribes were fighting to keep the British out of their valleys. On the twelfth of September, several thousand tribal fighters surrounded the post. Popular retellings say the defenders were offered safe passage if they gave it up. They stayed, and held for hours against far greater numbers. The signaler, Gurmukh Singh, kept flashing messages to the fort, reporting the fight as it happened, until the very end. Then, the story goes, he asked permission to leave his post, picked up his rifle, and fought until he fell. All twenty-one died. Each was given the highest gallantry award then open to Indian soldiers. Sikhs, and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army today, remember the twelfth of September as Saragarhi Day, and often tell it alongside the old Khalsa stories of saint-soldiers who stood their ground. Remember too that the men on the other side were fighting for their own homes. The lesson Sikhs draw isn't about them. It's about twenty-one people who stayed at a small post when staying mattered.

297.title: Jallianwala Bagh, Vaisakhi 1919
297.hook: British troops fire on an unarmed crowd in a walled garden in Amritsar, killing hundreds
297.howItsDone: The Jallianwala Bagh is a national memorial in Amritsar, near Harmandir Sahib; each year on 13 April, Vaisakhi, people gather there to remember those killed, and many Sikhs include them in their Vaisakhi remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saragarhi: twenty-one held. Today, Amritsar on its happiest day of the year, and what happened there.

Vaisakhi afternoon, 1919, in Amritsar. Thousands of people sit on the grass in a public garden a few minutes' walk from the Golden Temple. Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival, and for Sikhs the birthday of the Khalsa. The city is full: families in from the villages, bright turbans and scarves, a visit to the Harmandir, food, music, fairs. Some in the garden have come to hear speeches. Many have just come in from the festival to sit down.
screen: `VAISAKHI, 1919, AMRITSAR.` → `THOUSANDS ON THE GRASS.` → `A GARDEN NEAR THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Bagh means garden. Jallianwala Bagh was open ground in the middle of the city, closed in on all sides by the walls of houses, with only a few narrow ways in and out. That spring, Punjab was tense. There had been protests against new British laws allowing arrest without trial; two popular local leaders, one Hindu and one Muslim, had been arrested; public meetings had been banned. Many in the garden, especially the visitors from villages, likely didn't know about the ban. The crowd was Sikh, Hindu and Muslim together, and it was unarmed. A British officer, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, arrived with troops, stationed them at the main entrance, and without any warning ordered them to fire into the crowd. The firing went on for about ten minutes, until the ammunition was nearly spent. People tried to climb the walls. Some jumped into a well to escape. The official British count was 379 killed; Indian estimates were far higher, around a thousand. Many more were wounded. Nobody knows the true number. The massacre shocked India and many in Britain. The poet Rabindranath Tagore gave back his knighthood in protest, and that afternoon is often described as a turning point on the road to Indian independence. The garden is a memorial now, with bullet marks still in the walls and the well. And Amritsar's spring festival carries a second memory: each Vaisakhi, people gather in the garden to remember that afternoon.

298.title: Nankana Sahib, 1921
298.hook: reformers seeking to free gurdwaras from corrupt keepers are killed at Guru Nanak's birthplace
298.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the martyrs of Nankana Sahib each February, and the jand tree where Bhai Lachhman Singh was killed is preserved at Gurdwara Janam Asthan; pilgrims from India travel there for Guru Nanak's birth anniversary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jallianwala Bagh: vaisakhi, remembered. Today, two years later, a different kind of struggle, and a vow not to strike back.

A family keeps one precious place: the house where a great-great-grandmother was born. The caretaker hired to look after it starts treating it as his own. He charges people to come in and does as he likes inside. When the family complains, the authorities side with him. What would you do? In the early 1920s, many Sikhs faced that question about their historic gurdwaras, including the one where Guru Nanak was born.
screen: `A FAMILY'S PRECIOUS PLACE.` → `A CARETAKER WHO ACTS LIKE THE OWNER.` → `GURU NANAK'S BIRTHPLACE.`

segments.voice: Akali means one who belongs to Akal, the Timeless: the old name for God you met at the Akal Takht. In the 1920s it became the name of a movement. By then many historic gurdwaras were run by mahants, hereditary custodians who had come to treat the shrines and their lands as private property. Some ran them well. Others let in practices that went against the Gurus' teaching, and some were accused of corruption and worse. The colonial government mostly backed them. So Sikhs formed jathas, bands of volunteers, to take the gurdwaras back into community care, and they made a vow: no violence, even if attacked. At dawn on the twentieth of February, 1921, a jatha led by Bhai Lachhman Singh went to Gurdwara Janam Asthan at Nankana Sahib, the place of Guru Nanak's birth, to pray and ask for its handover. The mahant had prepared. His hired men shut the gates and attacked the Sikhs with guns, swords and axes. The jatha did not fight back. The counts differ: official figures were lower, and Sikh accounts say well over a hundred were killed. Bhai Lachhman Singh was tied to a tree and burned; the tree still stands at the gurdwara. The news shook all of India. Leaders came from across the country, and the government was forced to act against the mahant. Within days, the shrine passed into the care of a Sikh committee. The vow had held: peaceful, and firm.

299.title: The gurdwaras return, 1925
299.hook: after years of peaceful protest a law hands historic gurdwaras to an elected Sikh body
299.tomorrow: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars
299.howItsDone: The SGPC, elected by Sikh voters, manages the Harmandir Sahib and many historic gurdwaras in Punjab and neighboring states; it also publishes the Sikh Rehat Maryada.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akali volunteers at Nankana Sahib: peaceful, and firm. Today, where that vow led.

Every morning, a group of men walks down a country road toward a gurdwara's garden, to cut firewood for its kitchen. Every morning, police stop them and beat them with long sticks. The men don't raise a hand. They fall, get up if they can, and are carried away. The next morning, a new group walks the same road. And the next. Visitors come from far away just to watch, and can't believe it.
screen: `EVERY MORNING, THE SAME ROAD.` → `BEATEN, AND NOT STRIKING BACK.` → `THE NEXT MORNING, A NEW GROUP.`

segments.voice: SGPC stands for the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. Shiromani means foremost, supreme; parbandhak means managing. Sikhs formed it in November 1920, at the Akal Takht, to take the historic shrines back from the mahants and run them for the whole community. At first the government refused to recognize it. So began years of what Sikhs call morchas, peaceful campaigns. In the keys affair of 1921, the government took the keys to the Golden Temple's treasury. Sikhs protested without violence, in huge numbers, until the keys were handed back to the Sikh leader Baba Kharak Singh. Gandhi sent a telegram hailing it as a first victory in India's struggle for freedom. Then came the road in the hook: Guru ka Bagh, 1922, the garden of a gurdwara near Amritsar. Day after day, bands of volunteers walked to cut wood, were beaten by police, and did not strike back. An English clergyman, C. F. Andrews, went to see it, and wrote that he had witnessed something like a new heroism, born of suffering without retaliation. Thousands were arrested over those years; many were injured, and some died. Then, in 1925, the government passed the Sikh Gurdwaras Act. The historic gurdwaras of Punjab would be run by an elected Sikh body, which became the SGPC, and Sikh men and women would vote for it. It still runs the Harmandir and many other gurdwaras today. The vow from Nankana Sahib had held for years, through beatings and prison. And it worked.

300.title: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars
300.hook: tens of thousands of Sikhs served and many died in both world wars, far from Punjab
300.howItsDone: Sikhs remember their soldiers of both world wars at memorials in France, Britain and Punjab and at Remembrance Day services, where Sikh groups often lay wreaths and say Ardas for the fallen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the SGPC: peaceful protest worked. Today is day three hundred on this path. Thank you for walking it. And today, Sikhs who walked a very long way from home.

Autumn, 1914. A young farmer from a village in Punjab steps off a ship in France. He had never seen the sea before this journey, never felt cold like this. Within days he's in a muddy trench in Flanders, in a war between European empires he'd barely heard of a year ago, his turban under the gray sky. In his pocket, maybe, a small book of prayers. At home, his mother is waiting for a letter.
screen: `AUTUMN, 1914, FRANCE.` → `A PUNJABI FARMER IN A TRENCH.` → `HIS MOTHER WAITING FOR A LETTER.`

segments.voice: When the First World War began, India was ruled by Britain, and the Indian Army was sent to fight. Sikhs made up a large part of it, far more than their share of India's population. They were among the first Indian troops to reach the Western Front in 1914, holding lines at Ypres and fighting at Neuve Chapelle. Others served at Gallipoli, in Mesopotamia, in East Africa. Tens of thousands of Sikhs served, and many never came home. Many of their letters home survive, because army censors copied out and translated extracts. They talk about the cold, the guns, friends lost, and again and again about God and the village. Some ask the family to keep praying at the gurdwara. Twenty-five years later it happened again. In the Second World War, Sikh soldiers fought in North Africa, Italy, Malaya and the jungles of Burma, where a Sikh soldier named Nand Singh won the Victoria Cross, Britain's highest award for bravery. Why did they go? Historians give many answers. Many came from farming families, and soldiering was steady pay and honored work. Many had a strong military tradition and a sense of duty. Most were volunteers, though not all went freely. And it's a hard truth that they fought for an empire that did not let their own people rule themselves. For a long time, their part was mostly left out of the story of the wars. That's changing: there are memorials to Sikh soldiers in France, in Britain and in Punjab. They served and died far from Punjab, and they're remembered.

301.title: Partition, 1947
301.hook: Punjab is split; millions flee on both sides, many are killed, and Nankana Sahib is left in Pakistan
301.howItsDone: Sikh families remember Partition in stories passed down at home, and the daily Ardas asks for open access to the gurdwaras left in Pakistan; groups of Sikh pilgrims travel there for gurpurabs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fauji: far from Punjab. Today the story comes home to Punjab itself, and it's a hard one, so this one goes slowly.

Ask a Punjabi grandparent where the family comes from, and sometimes you get two answers: where we live now, and where we lived before. Before might be a village near Lahore, or Rawalpindi, or Lyallpur, a place they never saw again. In August 1947, British rule in India ended, and the land was divided. A new country, Pakistan, was made, and its border ran straight through the middle of Punjab. On one side, a family's fields, their well, their gurdwara. On the other, their new life, if they got there.
screen: `WHERE WE LIVED BEFORE.` → `AUGUST 1947.` → `A LINE THROUGH PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: The line was drawn by a British lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, in about five weeks. It was published two days after independence, and millions of people woke up on the wrong side of it. Muslims went west into Pakistan; Hindus and Sikhs went east into India. Across Punjab alone, something like ten million people crossed. How many died, nobody knows exactly: estimates run from a few hundred thousand to perhaps two million. Trains arrived carrying the dead. Women were taken from their families. And this lesson holds on to one thing: the violence came from every side. Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs all suffered, and people from every community did terrible things, so no people as a whole is to blame. There are also stories, on both sides of the line, of neighbors who hid neighbors and walked them to safety. For Sikhs there was a particular loss. Punjab was the land of the Gurus, and the line cut it in half. Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, was now in Pakistan. So was Kartarpur, where he farmed and died, and Panja Sahib, and the place in Lahore where Guru Arjan was martyred. In Punjabi, Partition is often called simply the vand, the division. For many families it isn't history at all. It's a grandmother's silence in August, a village name said softly at a kitchen table.
